title: Rabbi Yose HaGelili
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: Rabbi Yose HaGelili. Hyman writes: Of this great Tanna, who is mentioned in the Mishnah twenty-five times, neither his family nor his ancestors is known to us, nor from whom he received his Torah. When he came for the first time before Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva, he was already a great man of the generation, and this was at Yavneh, as stated explicitly in Zevachim 57a; this is a sign that he had already received his Torah from his teachers in the Galilee.

Hyman considers it close to the truth that Rabbi Yose HaGelili was already a great man of the generation even before the destruction, like his colleagues Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Eliezer; but he was not in the midst of the upheaval. Hyman writes that, as is well known, Roman violence did not afflict Galilee as it did Judea, and in many places the sword did not pass over them at all because they accepted Roman rule (כס״פי). And there

fled Rabbi Azaryah, the father of Rabbi Elazar, with his son, who was then young, and he entrusted him to Rabbi Yose HaGelili to teach him Torah. This is what we find in the Jerusalem Talmud, Ketubot 11:3, that Rabbi Yose HaGelili had a wicked wife (and in Bereshit Rabbah 17:3 it is explicit that she was his sister’s daughter), and she distressed him greatly. Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, who saw how much his teacher was distressed, said to him: “My teacher! Leave her and give her a bill of divorce.” He said to him: “I cannot,

for her ketubah is large.” He said to him: “I will give it to you” (for Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah was very wealthy, as is known; and we also find that his fixed place was in Tzippori, as in Tosefta Kelim, Bava Batra, chapter 2, which is in the Galilee). In Hyman’s reconstruction, apparently Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, immediately after the destruction, when they gathered at Yavneh and rested from war, then came there, and at about eighteen years old merited to ascend the seat of the patriarchate; but Rabbi Yose HaGelili remained

in his place many years. Hyman therefore judges the Rambam to be right in his Introduction to Zera’im in counting Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah in the second group after the destruction and Rabbi Yose HaGelili in the third group, since almost nothing of the names of the sages of the generation who were in the Galilee or in other lands remains to us, apart from the sages of Jerusalem and the sages of Yavneh; therefore it is not known to us who Rabbi Yose HaGelili’s teachers were and the days of

his activity there. Rabbi Yose HaGelili’s days of activity are counted only afterward, when he came to Yavneh, which was a long time afterward; therefore he is counted in the generation after Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, although Rabbi Yose HaGelili had been Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah’s teacher in the latter’s youth. This is what is related in Zevachim 57a and Sifrei Korach 42: when a question was asked in the vineyard at Yavneh … Rabbi Tarfon answered … there was a student there who had come to the study house before the sages for the first time, and Rabbi

Yose HaGelili was his name. He said to him: “My teacher, from where do you have this?” And then he showed his power and strength before Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva. Hyman considers it very likely that Rabbi Akiva was much older than he, since he lived long; therefore Rabbi Akiva called him “my son” there. Likewise we find in the Tosefta, end of Mikvaot, and Sifrei Chukkat 33, that Rabbi Tarfon said: “I saw the ram goring — that is Rabbi Akiva; and behold the he-goat came from the south

— that is Rabbi Yose HaGelili.” Indeed Rabbi Akiva esteemed him greatly and said to him: “Not to every person (would I retract), but to you, for you are Yose HaGelili.” In Chagigah 14a he said to Rabbi Akiva: “Akiva, how long will you make the Divine Presence profane?” In Zevachim 82a and Sifra Emor 7 he said to Rabbi Akiva: “Even if you multiply arguments all day long, I will not listen to you.” He likewise disagrees with Rabbi Akiva, as in Pesachim 7:1,

Ketubot 3:3, Bava Kamma 8:6, Sanhedrin 10:6, Makkot 2:7 and Bekhorot 2:6; with Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva, as in Parah 3:4, Niddah 5:8 and Horayot 2:5 — and in all of them Rabbi Yose HaGelili is mentioned first, except Sotah 8:5, Eruvin 96a, Rosh Hashanah 14a and Menachot 36b, where Rabbi Akiva is mentioned first.

In Menachot 5:8 he disagrees with Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel about what a marcheshet and a machavat are. Likewise he disagrees with the anonymous Mishnah, as in Eruvin 1:7, Gittin 2:3 and Bekhorot, beginning of chapter 8; and with the sages, Bekhorot 2:6, Zevachim 8:2 and 13:2, and Parah 1:2. And what we find in Kiddushin 39 and Menachot 38b,

that he spoke in the name of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri — Hyman explains that Yose was not Yochanan ben Nuri’s student; rather, they were colleagues, and he heard from him these two halakhot that he had received from Rabbi Eliezer the Great. His well-known halakhot: Berakhot 7:3, where he said, “According to the size of the assembly they bless.” Bikkurim 1:10: “One does not bring first fruits from across the Jordan.” Pesachim 32a: “Chametz on Passover is permitted for benefit.”

Ketubot 3:3: “A young woman who was betrothed and divorced is not entitled to a fine.” Bava Kamma 8:6: “For humiliation, he pays according to his standing.” There, 13a: “Lesser holy things are the owners’ property” (and Ben Azzai disagrees with him). There, 15a: “A tam [ox] pays half ransom.” Bava Metzia 2:10: “If there was more than

its load on it, he is not obliged to assist it.” Sanhedrin 10:7: “A condemned city — one may not make of it even gardens and orchards.” Shevuot 21a: “A prohibition involving no action — one is not flogged for it, except for one who swears, one who substitutes one sacrificial animal for another, and one who curses his fellow with the Name.” Avodah Zarah 3:5: “A thing attached to the ground is not forbidden through idolatry.”

Chullin 8:4: “Cooking fowl in milk is not from the Torah”; and in Shabbat 130a, that it is permitted even rabbinically, and in his place they ate fowl in milk. Bekhorot, beginning of chapter 8: if he married a maidservant who was freed, or a gentile woman who converted (although she had given birth while a gentile), the first son she bore him afterward is a firstborn for inheritance and for the Kohen.

He is likewise mentioned in Sheviit 4:6 and Chullin 5:3. Hyman writes that we always find him with the four elders, as in Moed Katan 28b: when the sons of Rabbi Yishmael died, four elders came in to comfort him: Rabbi Tarfon, Rabbi Yose HaGelili, Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah and Rabbi Akiva. In Gittin 83a: after the death of Rabbi Eliezer, four elders came in to respond to his words: Rabbi Yose HaGelili,

Rabbi Tarfon, Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah and Rabbi Akiva … Rabbi Yehoshua said to them: “One does not respond to a lion after his death.” In Sifrei Ekev, on “And it shall be”: “And Rabbi Tarfon, Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva were once reclining, and they asked: Is study greater?” In Kiddushin 40b the word HaGelili is missing. In Sifra Metzora 152 we find that he disagrees with Ben Azzai and says to him, “Explain it”; Ben Azzai said to him: “One does not

explain to a sage.” He said to him, “Recite it”; he said to him: “One does not recite to a sage.” The Yalkut, Chukkat, on “And Elazar shall take,” cites that once Rabbi Yose HaGelili was sitting and expounding the [red] heifer in Tiberias, and Rabbi Shimon ben Chanina was with him. In aggadah we do not find much of his, but the words he said are very precious, as in Sanhedrin 72b, where he gives a reason for the law of the rebellious son and says: “The Torah foresaw

where his thinking would ultimately lead,” etc. There, 90a: “The Torah foresaw where idolatry would ultimately lead.” In Niddah 31a: “Come and see that the measure of the Holy One, blessed be He, is not like the measure of flesh and blood … but the Holy One, blessed be He, forms the fetus in a woman’s womb, and all of them come out as one kind.” In Vayikra Rabbah 9:9 he said: “Great is peace,” etc.

Of his precious qualities we find that he was praised by Issi ben Yehudah in Avot deRabbi Natan, end of chapter 18, that he gathers well, well, without arrogance. His name remained a blessing in the mouth of later generations, as in Berakhot 5:2 and Taanit 1:1: “Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said: When Israel come to transgressions … the rains are withheld, and they bring them an elder such as Rabbi Yose HaGelili, and he intercedes

for them, and immediately the rains fall.” And the well-known story in Ketubot 11:3 of how he supported his wicked divorced wife. Of those who speak in his name we find Rabbi Elazar, in Zevachim 44a; Rabbi Yehudah, as in Shevuot 21a; Abba Yose ben Dostai, as in Tosefta Taanit, chapter 2;

Rabbi Yose ben Durmaskah (דורמסקה), in Kiddushin 39a; Rabbi Natan, as in Menachot 38b; and Rabbi Shimon ben Eliezer, as in Chullin 75a. In Eruvin 53b it is related of him that once he was walking on the road and found Beruryah (the daughter of Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon). He said to her, “By which road shall we go to Lod?” She said to him: “Foolish Galilean, did not the sages say: Do not converse much with a woman?”

Hyman lists three sons: one who died in his lifetime, as in Semachot, chapter 10; Rabbi Eliezer (Rabbi Yehudah’s colleague), as in Berakhot 63b; and Rabbi Chanina, a great man of the generation in the time of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel at Usha, as in Rosh Hashanah 32a. Hyman writes: We find no account of his death anywhere; apparently he went to the Galilee before the destruction of Betar, and there he died.

notes.text: Root read the complete supplied Hebrew, all 22 current/proposed English units, all current and historical notes and the named evidence. Sentences continue across line-group units. Hyman owns the chronological, geographical and teacher-student reconstruction, including its assertions and qualifications; this is not canonical genealogy. The supplied כס״פי remains a tentative Josephus reference, not a verified expansion. The wife episode is supplied first as JT Ketubot 1:3 and later as 11:3; the saved Guggenheimer 11:3 whole paragraph matches the episode and calls Elazar ben Azaryah’s addressee רבי, rendered vocatively as my teacher. That does not independently establish Hyman’s earlier-life chronology. The supplied Vayikra Rabbah locator פ״יטט is retained, rather than silently asserted as 9:9; the saved Midrash Rabbah--TE 9:9 paragraph does contain Yose HaGelili’s Great is peace. Durmaskah follows supplied דורמסקה, not silent Durmaskit harmonization. The final היינו דר׳ יהודה is kept literally as of Rabbi Yehudah and remains unclear; the saved Davidson Berakhot63b names Eliezer son of Yose HaGelili, but cannot authorize replacing the supplied parenthesis or claiming a printed-page error. The Eruvin53b Beruryah encounter was checked in the saved whole paragraph. Supplemental Davidson Niddah31a paragraph12 confirms the shortened quotation ending all emerge as one kind; paragraph13 is a separate alternative, not a reason to reverse the supplied quotation. All earlier note questions survive; these three units remain held for supplied siglum/locator/parenthesis questions. Digital evidence is not printed pixels or correction history.

The he-goat comes “from the south” (מן הנגב) in the supplied wording. That wording is preserved within Hyman’s cited image; it has not been harmonized to a different biblical direction or used to infer an OCR history.

The following comparisons concern selected digital witnesses. Hyman’s historical reconstruction and textual proposals remain attributed to him; unresolved differences are recorded without silently changing his Hebrew or references. These comparisons are not a collation of every edition or an independent reconstruction of Yose HaGelili’s life.

In the consulted Zevachim 57a sequence, Tarfon gives the first answer and the “my son” exchange occurs before Akiva enters the discussion. Hyman’s attribution of that address to Akiva is retained as his account, with this witness difference unresolved. The wife narratives in Jerusalem Talmud Ketubot 11:3 and Bereshit Rabbah 17:3 support the address “Rabbi,” the divorce settlement, and subsequent support; Bereshit Rabbah explicitly calls the wife his sister’s daughter and has a plural offer of payment, beside the Jerusalem Talmud’s singular offer. These passages do not independently establish Hyman’s reconstruction of Elazar ben Azaryah’s childhood, refuge in Galilee, or early schooling.

The consulted Tosefta Mikvaot 8:6 supports the dispute, retraction, and ram-and-goat comparison, but its goat comes “from the west,” beside Hyman’s supplied southern/Negev wording. Neither wording is silently substituted for the other, and no biographical direction is established from the image. Sifra, Emor, Section 7:2 includes the “even if you multiply all day” exchange with explicit editorial brackets reporting reversed Gemara speaker attributions. The forms and attribution differences remain distinct; no canonical speaker correction is made.

Several summaries and references require the same caution. In the consulted Bava Kamma 8:6, Yehudah reports Yose HaGelili’s maneh award, while the following rule about a person’s honor is anonymous in that witness. Sanhedrin 10:6 contains the gardens-and-orchards dispute beside Hyman’s supplied 10:7 reference; literal digital 10:7 was unavailable in the consulted route. Zevachim 8:2 and 44a did not independently establish the intended named claims in the bounded passages checked. Parah 3:4, Niddah 5:8, and Horayot 2:5 name Yose HaGelili and Akiva without Tarfon in those particular segments; Hyman’s collective list is not a claim newly verified for each segment. The consulted quotations in Eruvin 96a, Rosh Hashanah 14a, and Menachot 36b put Yose HaGelili’s stated opinion before Akiva’s, although Eruvin’s preceding framing names Akiva. Hyman’s observation about order is retained as his textual observation, rather than certified across all editions.

Occurrence forms are preserved: the consulted Menachot 5:8 has Chananyah ben Gamliel beside Hyman’s Chanina, and Chullin 75a has Shimon ben Elazar beside the supplied Shimon ben Eliezer. Plain “Rabbi Yose” is not automatically identified with Yose HaGelili. Niddah 31a’s image of all coming out one kind and its separately introduced alternative of each coming out its own kind are not merged. Berakhot 63b explicitly names Eliezer son of Yose HaGelili; Hyman’s unresolved Yehudah parenthesis is retained. Semachot 10 independently reports a son’s death without identifying that son. Yalkut Shimoni on Torah 761:3 supports the Tiberias red-heifer discussion with Shimon ben Chanina; the rain passages in Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 5:2 and Taanit 1:1 give the example of an elder such as Yose HaGelili interceding. These comparisons do not establish further family, pupil, or chronological relations.

Hyman’s edition-specific Sifrei Korach/Chukkat and Sifra Metzora pointers, the Tosefta Kelim Tzippori report, Rambam’s generational grouping, the twenty-five-Mishnah count, printed readings and sigla, the Josephus identification, and the reconstruction of age, teachers, Galilean residence, and death before Betar have not been independently collated or established here. Unmatched routes, unavailable catalogue entries, and search results are not proof that a passage or work is absent. Those reports remain attributed and unresolved, with the Hebrew, titles, references, and existing notes preserved.

The earlier notes tentatively associate the supplied shorthand כס״פי with Josephus. The exact expansion and the passage Hyman intended remain uncertain after inspection of the printed page. For comparison, in Jewish War 3.2.4 and 3.4.1 Josephus describes Sepphoris making terms and also describes severe Roman violence elsewhere in Galilee. These episodes provide context for Hyman’s account. His reconstruction of Rabbi Yose’s life and the flight of Rabbi Azaryah and his son remain his own.

The first reference is Ketubot 1:3 in the supplied Hebrew. Hyman’s printed volume II, p. 738, gives 11:3, as does the later citation. The wife episode is in Jerusalem Talmud Ketubot 11:3, where Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah addresses Rabbi Yose as “Rabbi.” Hyman draws a further inference about their earlier relationship.
The supplied Hebrew locator is פ״יטט. Hyman’s printed volume II, p. 739, gives Vayikra Rabbah 9:9, where Rabbi Yose HaGelili praises peace and says that even in war one begins by offering peace.

The supplied Hebrew has היינו דר׳ יהודה in this parenthesis. Hyman’s printed volume II, p. 740, reads חבירו דר׳ יהודה, “Rabbi Yehudah’s colleague.” Berakhot 63b places Rabbi Eliezer with Rabbi Yehudah at Yavne and names Eliezer as the son of Rabbi Yose HaGelili. Semachot 10 gives no name for the son who died in his father’s lifetime. Rosh Hashanah 32a names Chanina as Yose HaGelili’s son and places his service as prayer leader at Usha.
